summary: Gives example SIP messages designed to push a SIP implementation hard, with odd but valid or invalid forms to test parsers. Implementers can use them to find bugs. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A set of tricky exam questions for a program that reads messages, to see whether it gets confused by strange but allowed wording.

questions: how to test a sip parser
is a percent sign an escape in sip
subtitle: A seed collection of nasty but instructive SIP messages for finding bugs in parsers and applications.

tldr.problem: SIP is a text protocol with a flexible grammar, and implementations repeatedly stumbled on odd but legal input and on malformed input at SIPit interoperability events.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists test messages, each with a note on what makes it unusual and how a receiving element should react, grouped into valid parser tests, invalid parser tests, transaction and application-layer tests, and a backward-compatibility test.
tldr.outcome: It is a seed for a test plan rather than a test plan, and it is not normative on any aspect of SIP. Implementers use it to harden parsers against both accidents and crafted input.

facts.label: Appendix A
facts.value: Base-64 gzip-compressed TAR of every message

today: RFC 4475 is Informational, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It stays a source of test cases for the behavior defined in RFC 3261, and it is explicitly not a specification.

sections.title: What the Torture Tests Are
sections.content:
RFC 4475 gives example messages for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) that are meant to exercise and "torture" an implementation. The document is informational and NOT NORMATIVE on any aspect of SIP. The messages are based on SIP 2.0 as defined in RFC 3261, and some also use the Session Description Protocol as described in RFC 3264.

The messages were developed and refined at the SIPIt interoperability test events. The RFC does not try to list every way to build an invalid message, or every unusual but valid one. It focuses on areas that caused interoperability problems or that are especially harmful when handled badly, and calls itself a seed for a test plan, not a test plan in itself.
sections.eli5: Imagine a spelling test full of tricky words. These messages are tricky words for a SIP program, picked because real programs got them wrong.

sections.title: Markup Used to Write Messages Down
sections.content:
Some SIP messages cannot be shown unambiguously in an RFC because of line-length limits and non-printable characters, so the document defines a small markup. It borrows XML-style tags but defines no XML document type.

  • <allOneLine/> marks text that is one long unfolded line. A reader joins the lines between the tags by direct concatenation, and any whitespace at a fold point appears at the start of a line.
  • <hex/> shows octets as pairs of hexadecimal digits, for binary bodies and non-ASCII UTF-8 characters.
  • <repeat count=N/> repeats a value, so very large values can be written compactly.

This is not SIP header-line folding, where different strings of bits have equivalent meaning. To settle any remaining doubt, Appendix A carries a bit-exact archive of every message.
sections.eli5: The authors made a few shorthand marks, like writing "3 times" instead of repeating a word, so the odd messages fit on the page. A secret file at the end holds the exact versions.

sections.title: Valid but Strange Messages
sections.content:
The first group is well-formed messages that look wrong. A receiver must accept them. The first, a "short tortuous INVITE", has line folding everywhere, whitespace around colons and semicolons, a mix of short and long header names, unusual capitalization, and integer fields such as Max-Forwards and CSeq with leading zeros. It also has an unknown header, UnknownHeaderWithUnusualValue, whose value would be invalid if it followed the generic parameter syntax. Because the receiver does not know that header's definition, it must parse it as a plain value, proxies forward it unchanged and endpoints ignore it.

Other valid tests cover a wide range of legal characters in a method name, escaped nulls in a URI, and a long list of header values. Several of them target the % character. In most places in a SIP message it is not an escape character: a method of IN%56ITE is an unknown method, not INVITE, and unescaping is never recursive, so value%41 is not valueA. Implementations must also take care that an escaped null does not shorten a user name early.

The group also includes extra trailing octets in a UDP datagram, which must be ignored as noise, varied and unknown transport types, a multipart MIME message, and responses with an unusual or an empty reason phrase.
sections.eli5: These messages look broken but are actually allowed, like a sentence with odd spacing and capital letters that is still correct. The program has to read them anyway.

sections.title: Invalid Messages and Reactions
sections.content:
The second group is deliberately broken, and each test names what is wrong. Examples include extra separators in a Via header, a Content-Length larger than the message or negative, an unterminated quoted string, a Request-URI wrapped in <>, spaces inside a URI, repeated spaces in the request line, an invalid time zone in a Date header, an unknown protocol version, a start line that disagrees with the CSeq method, and an overlarge response code.

The RFC also says how an element should usually react. A request with a bad Via or a mismatched Content-Length over UDP should get a 400 Bad Request. A request whose CSeq is above 2**32-1 should get a 400, while an out-of-range Max-Forwards alone could be treated as absent, and bad expiry values could fall back to the default of 3600. A response with out-of-range scalar fields is simply discarded. Where a lenient parser might try to repair input, such as inferring a closing quote, the RFC warns that it must make a reasonable inference.
sections.eli5: These are the messages that are truly wrong, like a letter with no address. The right move is usually to politely say "that is not valid", and never to crash.

sections.title: Transaction, Application and Compatibility Tests
sections.content:
The next tests go beyond parsing and also exercise the logic above it. One has a branch parameter with the z9hG4bK prefix but no identifier after it. The element could reject it with a 400, preferably statelessly, or fall back to the older RFC 2543-style transaction identifier. Another request is missing Call-ID, From and To, and the receiver must not break and ideally answers 400.

Several tests cover extension and routing rules. A request listing unsupported features in Require and Proxy-Require draws a 420 Bad Extension with an Unsupported header. A request with Max-Forwards of zero should not be forwarded by a proxy, which should answer 483 (Too Many Hops), while an endpoint processes it normally. A response whose second Via carries the broadcast address 255.255.255.255 should be dropped by proxies so that it cannot be used as an attack route.

The last test is an INVITE in RFC 2543 syntax, with no branch parameter, no From tag, no explicit Content-Length and no Max-Forwards. RFC 3261 elements that want backward compatibility should accept it.
sections.eli5: Here the tricks are about what the message asks for, not how it is spelled. A hop counter reaching zero means stop passing it along, and an old-style message should still be understood.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The messages are non-normative examples, and the security considerations of RFC 3261 apply. The RFC points out that attacks on many Internet systems use crafted input, and that many of these messages stress a parser exactly where such attacks traditionally land. It adds that the document is not comprehensive and should be a seed to stimulate thinking and planning, not just a set of tests to pass.
sections.eli5: Bad guys often send weird messages to make programs misbehave. Practicing with weird messages first helps a program stay safe, but passing these tests is not a promise of safety.
